findings.title: `listener_misses` FK to `listeners` has no delete policy, so three existing listener deletes will fail
findings.why_it_matters: The Storage bullet says only "listener id (FK to `listeners`)". Foreign keys are enforced, and the default action is NO ACTION. Any `DELETE FROM listeners` for a listener that has miss rows will raise an IntegrityError. The stale-`once` cleanup rolls back its whole transaction and logs "Failed to clean up stale once=True listeners" on every startup. The retention parent-guard delete propagates the error out of the retention transaction, which stalls every retention cycle and leaves the database to grow.
findings.recommended: B: `ON DELETE CASCADE` on `listener_misses.listener_id`, and name it in the Storage bullet
findings.chosen: B: `ON DELETE CASCADE` on `listener_misses.listener_id`, and name it in the Storage bullet

findings.title: Upsert and flush semantics are unspecified, and the obvious reading corrupts counts
findings.why_it_matters: The unique index is on (listener, hour, reason, filter), but each process creates its in-memory entries fresh. If the upsert overwrites, a restart or app reload inside the hour starts the entry at 0, and the first flush replaces the row's count and `first_ts` with smaller values. If entries are cumulative and only "dirty" ones flush, closed-hour entries stay in memory for the process lifetime, each holding references to the last event's raw tracked values (the senior engineer's F8, eviction half).
findings.chosen: In the Flush bullet, state the following. An in-memory entry holds only what accrued since the last flush. At flush, the recorder swaps its entry map for an empty one, so dispatch writes to fresh entries and closed hours leave memory. The batch upserts with `count = count + excluded.count`, `first_ts = MIN(first_ts, excluded.first_ts)`, and the last-event columns replaced only when `excluded.last_ts >= last_ts`. A dropped or failed flush loses exactly that swapped-out batch.

findings.title: A failed flush can't be detected through fire-and-forget `enqueue`
findings.why_it_matters: The Posture says a failed flush is counted and warned once per episode. `DatabaseWriteQueue.enqueue` returns True as soon as the coroutine is queued, and a SQLite error when it later runs is only logged by the worker. Through `enqueue`, the recorder sees only queue-full, not-ready and yielded-to-`submit` drops. A disk-full, locked or constraint failure (for example Finding 1's) goes uncounted, and an empty `--misses` can't be told apart from "flush has been failing".
findings.chosen: In the Flush bullet, have the flush task await `DatabaseService.submit()` for its batch, as the execution flusher does (`execution_pipeline.py:280`). A raised SQLite error, a submit `TimeoutError` or an unavailable queue then reaches the recorder, which counts it and logs the WARNING once per episode. Entries are detached before the write (Finding 2) and lost on failure, with no retry, per Posture.

findings.title: Filter attribution must be the evaluation, not a second walk after the predicate returns False
findings.why_it_matters: `AllOf.__call__` returns one bool, and the ledger doesn't say whether the attribution walk replaces the `predicate(ev)` call or follows it. The low-diff reading calls the predicate, and on False walks the children again to find the culprit. That evaluates user `where` callables twice. For a time-of-day window, an "is anyone home" lookup or a counter, the second pass can find no rejecting child or blame the wrong one, so the row's "by which filter" is confidently wrong.
findings.chosen: In the Summary's "Filter attribution" bullet, state the following. `Listener.matches` evaluates the flattened user-facing children itself, once each, in order, stopping at the first false one. This replaces the call to the folded predicate, and no child is ever evaluated a second time to attribute a rejection. The loop costs the same as `all()` over a generator on the matching path.

findings.title: Record `debounce_superseded` where the previous task is superseded, not in the cancellation handler
findings.why_it_matters: `RateLimiter.call` receives only a zero-arg closure, so the superseded event isn't in hand unless RateLimiter keeps it. The natural place to record, `delayed_call`'s `except asyncio.CancelledError: return`, is also reached when `cancel()` runs at listener removal and when the task bucket is cancelled at shutdown. Recording there produces false `debounce_superseded` rows on every reload or shutdown with a pending debounce.
findings.chosen: In the "Drop reporting" bullet, state that `debounce_superseded` is recorded in `RateLimiter.debounced_call`, in the branch that cancels a still-pending previous task, for the event that task was holding. RateLimiter keeps that pending call's event (or drop report) next to `_debounce_task`. The `CancelledError` branch in `delayed_call` records nothing.

findings.title: A `hold_cancelled` row must record the original cancelling event, not the normalized copy
findings.why_it_matters: `evaluate_cancel_event` evaluates `eval_event`, a copy from `strip_old_state` with `old_state` set to None. D7 was ratified so that the row shows "`on` → `off` at 22:03". If the drop is reported with the event in hand at the predicate check, which is the normalized copy, the row loses the old value that D7 chose it for.
findings.chosen: In D7's Recommendation (and the "Drop reporting" bullet), state that `hold_cancelled` records the `event` that `evaluate_cancel_event` received, not the normalized copy it evaluates. Because this is an Auto-apply edit to D7, set D7's `**Ratified:**` back to `pending`.

findings.title: The shutdown flush must run after dispatch drains and before the write queue detaches
findings.why_it_matters: "Flush once on shutdown" doesn't say when. Dispatch tasks still pending at shutdown can add misses after the flush, and `enqueue`/`submit` raise once `DatabaseService` has detached its queue.
findings.chosen: At build: BusService's shutdown awaits dispatch idle, then runs the final flush awaited through the same `submit` path (Finding 3), all before DatabaseService detaches its queue.

findings.title: Under D2, an empty `--misses` can't mean "the listener saw nothing"
findings.why_it_matters: The Summary's stated problem is that "a listener showing 0 runs looks the same whether it rejected 500 events or never saw one." Under D2, a default `on_state_change`/`on_attribute_change` listener that only ever fails the default change filter still records nothing, so that ambiguity remains for the most common listener type. D2 accepted this ("a listener that only ever fails `changed=True` shows nothing"). The open part is that no doc tells the reader that an empty result is ambiguous.
findings.recommended: A: Keep D2 as ratified; the `workflows.md` walkthrough and `filtering.md` state that an empty `--misses` doesn't mean the listener saw no events
findings.chosen: A: Keep D2 as ratified; the `workflows.md` walkthrough and `filtering.md` state that an empty `--misses` doesn't mean the listener saw no events

findings.title: D2's `NOT_PROVIDED` default on `changed=` adds a signature change for one row an hour
findings.why_it_matters: D2-C exists to honor a caller who writes `changed=True` explicitly. `True` is today's default, so writing it out changes no dispatch behavior. The only difference C produces is recording those rejections, which D2's own table calls the busiest, least useful row. The cost is a sentinel default in two public signatures, wording in two docstrings and `methods.md`, and a three-way branch (sentinel, `True`, comparison) at registration. C infers a preference about recording from whether a default value was typed.

findings.title: Drop reporting through a per-dispatch closure vs. one reporter bound at registration
findings.why_it_matters: The Drop reporting bullet has BusService build a drop callback per dispatch that closes over the event and listener, and threads it into `HandlerInvoker.dispatch`, `RateLimiter.call` and the mode guard. Both critics prefer binding one reporter at registration and having drop sites pass `(reason, event)`. Their shared rationale, that the closure falls inside parent D3's 10% budget on rejected events, doesn't hold. Rejected events never reach `_dispatch`, so the closure is built only for events that already pay for an `invoke_fn` closure, a coroutine and a task spawn. What remains is a shape question: allocation on the dispatched path, and where the listener-to-recorder link lives.
findings.recommended: A: Bind one reporter to the listener's invoker at registration; drop sites pass `(reason, event)`
findings.chosen: A: Bind one reporter to the listener's invoker at registration; drop sites pass `(reason, event)`

findings.title: The 10% benchmark doesn't say what it measures or what it compares against
findings.why_it_matters: Parent D3's limit is "at most 10% added to rejected-event dispatch", but the ledger doesn't say what the 10% is a fraction of. Measured against `Listener.matches` alone (a sub-microsecond string compare), a dict update keyed by a tuple with a clock read can exceed it. Measured against the whole `_match_listeners` route-and-match pass, it likely won't. No dispatch benchmark exists today, so "before" means running the new file against pre-change code. The ledger doesn't say to commit it first or where to record the numbers. The senior engineer's volume argument (domain-topic fan-out makes rejections dominant) is weaker than stated: under D1, that fan-out is rejected at scope and never reaches the miss path.
findings.recommended: A: State in the Benchmark bullet what is timed and what the 10% is of; commit the benchmark before the recording code and record both numbers under the build calls
findings.chosen: A: State in the Benchmark bullet what is timed and what the 10% is of; commit the benchmark before the recording code and record both numbers under the build calls

findings.title: The two hold codes could ship as a follow-up instead of in this build
findings.why_it_matters: `hold_cancelled` and `hold_recheck_failed` need two more injection points (`DurationHoldManager` and `DurationTimer.evaluate_cancel_event`), and D7 exists only for them. That is a third of the decisions and two extra files, for duration listeners only, in a build that has to finish in one session. The recorder interface makes them additive later. Parent D4 says every listener-scoped drop counts, so dropping them is a scoping choice, not a fix.
findings.recommended: A: Keep `hold_cancelled` and `hold_recheck_failed` in this build as ratified
findings.chosen: A: Keep `hold_cancelled` and `hold_recheck_failed` in this build as ratified

findings.title: Two `where` children that render the same summary share one database row
findings.why_it_matters: In memory, entries are keyed by child position. In the database, the unique index uses the rendered summary. Two children that render the same way, such as two lambdas that both summarize as `<lambda>`, are two memory entries that collide on one database key in the same batch. With Finding 2's additive upsert they merge into one row instead of overwriting each other, so the count covers both filters and the last values come from whichever rejected last.
findings.recommended: B: Keep the rendered summary as the key; identically rendering children share one row
findings.chosen: B: Keep the rendered summary as the key; identically rendering children share one row

findings.title: D5's nine codes: the extra splits are the one-way part of the wire
findings.why_it_matters: Adding a reason code later is additive, because lenient wire fields absorb unknown values. Removing one is a wire break, as D5's own Reversibility line says. Starting at seven and splitting later is the free direction. Starting at nine and merging later is not. The critic would keep D3's filter-in-key and flags only D5.
findings.recommended: B: Accept as a known limitation: retiring any of the nine codes later is a wire break
findings.chosen: B: Accept as a known limitation: retiring any of the nine codes later is a wire break

findings.title: `hold_recheck_failed` doesn't say whether the state moved or the entity left the cache
findings.why_it_matters: D5 sells each code as pointing at the setting to change. `hold_recheck_failed` covers both "the state moved without an event" and "the entity is missing from the cache at fire time". Those have different fixes: the second usually means the entity was renamed or removed.
findings.recommended: B: Accept as a known limitation: a `hold_recheck_failed` row doesn't say whether the state moved or the entity left the cache
findings.chosen: B: Accept as a known limitation: a `hold_recheck_failed` row doesn't say whether the state moved or the entity left the cache
